subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage: The projector had died fifteen minutes into the lecture, so the professor was explaining eigenvalues on the whiteboard for three hundred students, and the back rows could barely hear. Jyoti had a question about the second example and kept it inside for forty minutes. Beside her, Sarita was doodling. “Last question,” the professor said, checking the clock. Jyoti's heart thudded. She put up her hand, the microphone was passed down the row, and her voice cracked as she asked. The professor answered. Behind her someone breathed out, “Thank God, I had the same one.” Two more students called out follow-ups. Sarita looked up from the doodle, grinning, and tapped Jyoti's notebook.

qa.q: How many students were in the lecture hall?
qa.a: There were three hundred students.

qa.q: What was Jyoti afraid of while she kept the question inside for forty minutes?
qa.a: Jyoti seems afraid of seeming ignorant in front of a huge hall, since her heart thudded and her voice cracked when she finally asked.

qa.q: What small step could help a student who holds back questions in a big lecture?
qa.a: They could write the question down early, sit nearer the front, or ask at the first pause instead of waiting for the last question.

qa.q: What might the person behind Jyoti have felt when saying, “Thank God, I had the same one”?
qa.a: That person probably felt relieved and grateful that Jyoti asked it, since they had held the same doubt without saying it.

grounding: A college student holds back a question in a large hall for fear of seeming ignorant and finds that others had the same question.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage: Maria's question about the tax-slab example had been sitting in her notebook since ten o'clock. In the lecture hall for two hundred, the professor asked, “Any doubts?” and the room stayed silent, as it always did. Everyone else understands, Maria thought, and kept her hand under her thigh. After class, in the canteen, Preeti pushed a plate of samosas toward her. “You looked puzzled. What was it?” When Maria told them, three others at the table said, “That confused me too!” and one asked, “Why didn't you ask?” Maria laughed at herself. Next morning she took a seat in the second row, and when the professor asked for doubts, hers was the first hand up.

qa.q: Where did Maria talk about her question after class?
qa.a: Maria talked about it in the canteen.

qa.q: Why did Maria keep her hand under her thigh when the professor asked, “Any doubts?”
qa.a: Maria assumed that everyone else understood and feared looking ignorant if she was the only one asking.

qa.q: What changed for Maria after the canteen talk?
qa.a: Maria learned that three others had the same doubt, laughed at herself, and next morning sat in the second row and asked first.

qa.q: What might Preeti have noticed about Maria that made Preeti ask, “What was it?”
qa.a: Preeti seems to have noticed the puzzled look on Maria's face and wanted to help, which fits pushing the plate over and asking kindly.

grounding: A college student holds back a question in a big hall, then finds in the canteen that others had the same doubt, and asks the next day.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage: The economics lecture hall held two hundred students, and Professor Samir Rao spoke fast. Aadhya had been confused since the second slide: why did the demand curve shift, instead of just moving along? She wrote the question in the margin of her notebook, then crossed it out. Everyone else seemed to be nodding. Her neighbour was scrolling on his phone. The professor asked, 'Any questions?' The hall went silent. Aadhya's heart was pounding. She raised her hand. 'Sorry, this may be basic, but why does the curve shift here instead of moving along it?' The professor smiled. 'Not basic at all. Most people mix these up.' He redrew the graph. Afterwards, three students she had never spoken to stopped her at the door. 'Thank you. I was lost on that too.'

qa.q: How many students did the lecture hall hold?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya cross the question out at first?
qa.a: She felt anxious about seeming ignorant, since everyone else seemed to be nodding.

qa.q: What could Aadhya tell herself before the next lecture?
qa.a: That if something confuses her, others are probably confused too, so asking helps the whole hall.

qa.q: How do the three students at the door experience Aadhya's question?
qa.a: They were lost too, and felt relieved and grateful that someone asked.

grounding: A college student overcomes the fear of seeming ignorant in a big hall and finds others shared the question.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage:
Hi Akash veerji,
You told me to ask questions in college. I tried, sort of. In organic chemistry there are three hundred of us, and the professor talks to the back wall. On Tuesday I didn't get why one reaction needed heat and the other didn't. I sat with my hand half up for maybe a whole minute, then pulled it down. I kept imagining everyone turning around and thinking, 'How did this one get admission?'
After class I went to the doubt board outside the department and found the same question already written by someone else, with six ticks next to it. Six people! I'd have been number seven.
So on Thursday I asked. My voice shook. Nobody laughed. Two people even wrote the answer down.
Amandeep

qa.q: How many ticks were next to the question on the doubt board?
qa.a: Six ticks.

qa.q: What was Amandeep afraid of on Tuesday?
qa.a: Amandeep felt afraid of seeming ignorant, imagining everyone turning around to wonder how Amandeep got admission.

qa.q: What made it easier for Amandeep to ask on Thursday?
qa.a: Seeing six others with the same question on the doubt board showed Amandeep wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might the two people who wrote down the answer feel about Amandeep's question?
qa.a: They were probably grateful, since it cleared up something they also needed.

grounding: A student holds back a question in a huge lecture, then learns many shared it and asks next time.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage: Payal, thanks for having me on campus radio. So, the question thing. I'm Baljeet, second-year engineering, and for a whole semester I never opened my mouth in the big lecture theatre. Two hundred and fifty people, a microphone on a stand, the professor squinting up at the rows. I'd rather fail than walk to that mic. Then one day in thermodynamics, the professor wrote an equation with a sign I was sure was wrong. My friend Gurmeet nudged me: 'Say it.' I didn't. Ten minutes later a first-year walked up and asked about the same sign. It was a mistake. The professor thanked the first-year, and the whole hall clapped. I felt stupid and relieved at the same time. The next week, I was the one at the mic.

qa.q: What did the first-year ask about?
qa.a: The same sign in the thermodynamics equation that Baljeet thought was wrong.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the first-year asked the question?
qa.a: Baljeet felt foolish for staying quiet and relieved at the same time, since the doubt had been right.

qa.q: What would you advise Baljeet about the fear of the microphone?
qa.a: Start with short questions and remember that others probably share them, as the clapping hall showed.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gurmeet, nudging Baljeet?
qa.a: Gurmeet may have felt frustrated seeing a friend hold back a correct doubt, and pleased when Baljeet finally went to the mic.

grounding: A student afraid of seeming ignorant stays silent until someone else asks the same question and the hall is grateful.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage:
Monday. In the two-hundred-seat hall, Professor Iyer raced through eigenvalues. Karthik's question sat in his throat: why does the matrix have to be square? He looked at the rows of nodding heads and wrote it in his margin instead, underlined twice. Beside him, Rehana was drawing tiny spirals.
Wednesday. The tutorial sheet was all square matrices, and Karthik was stuck on the first problem. In the canteen Rehana admitted she had copied the worked example without understanding a line. So had two others at their table.
Friday. Palms sweating, Karthik raised his arm halfway through the lecture. "Sorry, basic doubt: why must it be square?" A few heads turned. The professor smiled and spent five minutes on it. Afterwards, three strangers stopped him on the stairs. "Thanks, yaar. I've had that exact question since Monday."

qa.q: What was Karthik's question?
qa.a: Why the matrix has to be square.

qa.q: Why did Karthik write the question in his margin on Monday instead of asking it?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking ignorant in front of rows of nodding students, so embarrassment won over curiosity.

qa.q: What could Karthik remind himself before the next big lecture?
qa.a: If something confuses him, others are probably confused too, so asking early helps the whole hall, not just him.

qa.q: How did the three strangers on the stairs see Karthik's question?
qa.a: They were grateful and relieved, because they had carried the same doubt since Monday and hadn't dared to ask.

grounding: Shows a college student holding back a question in a big hall, then asking and finding others were grateful for it.
